## Psalm 125: verse-by-verse notes

### v. 1: "Those who trust in the LORD are like Mount Zion"

**Traditional reading**
- **Guzik (Enduring Word):** This is a promise only for those who trust in the LORD. You can't really trust Him while you still rely on other things. What follows is a promise made to those who put their trust in the LORD. We can't properly put our trust in Him until we remove our trust in other things. Pilgrims from far away were struck by the height and steadiness of Zion, and the believer is promised the same security.  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-125/
- **Spurgeon:** The focus is on who is trusted, the LORD Himself. The emphasis lies upon the object of their trust. God's people can't be moved by outside force or by their own fickleness.  https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps125.cfm
- **Matthew Henry:** Zion stands firm because providence holds it up, and even more because it is a holy mountain held up by God's promise. Believers can't be moved away from their integrity or from their confidence in God.  https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_125.cfm
- **Gill:** True trust is not in ourselves, our strength, wealth or righteousness, or in any creature, but in the Lord. The Targum reads "the Word of the Lord," which Gill applies to Christ.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/125.htm
- **Pulpit Commentary:** Read "*are* as Mount Zion" rather than "shall be." It compares Isaiah 28:16.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/125.htm
- **Maclaren (on the Biblehub commentary page):** A mountain surrounded by mountains suggests that faith, in some measure, makes the protected like the Protector. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/125-1.htm

### v. 2: "As the mountains surround Jerusalem"

**Traditional reading**
- **Guzik:** Because God surrounds His people, nothing can reach them without first passing through Him.  Verse 2 must not be separated from the condition of trust in verse 1.  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-125/
- **Spurgeon:** The hills are like sentinels, not prison walls.  He also notes that it is God Himself, not just His power, who surrounds believers.  https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps125.cfm
- **Geography:**
  - The Pulpit Commentary names the surrounding heights (Mount of Olives, Hill of Evil Counsel, Scopus) and says all are higher than the city.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/125.htm
  - Gill cites Kimchi: the hills did not stop enemies taking the city, so the Lord is a better protection.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/125.htm
- **Henry:** "For ever" points to final fulfilment in heaven (Rev. 3:12).  https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_125.cfm
- **A writer quoted in Spurgeon's *Treasury*:** "Henceforth, even for ever" shows that promises made to Israel pertain generally to the Church in every age. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tod/psalms-125.html

### v. 3: "The scepter of the wicked will not rest…"

**Traditional reading**
- **What "scepter" means:**
  - The Pulpit Commentary translates it literally as "the scepter of wickedness." The "lot" is the land the righteous live in, which may fall under wicked rule for a while but will not stay there.  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-125.html
  - Gill lists several possible meanings: a rod of correction, a scepter (which he applies to antichrist), a tribe, or (his preference, following Gussetius) a measuring rod laid on land and estates.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/125.htm
- **Why God limits wicked rule:** if oppression lasts too long, it could push even good people into sin.
  - Henry: God considers the frame of his people, and will proportion their trials to their strength. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_125.cfm
  - Spurgeon: God's people should not expect to escape trial, and the rod may light on their portion, but it shall not rest upon it. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps125.cfm
  - Guzik quotes Trapp, who quotes Chrysostom: God is like a lute player who keeps the strings neither too slack nor too tight.  He adds that the scepter rested on the land only when Israel was stubbornly unfaithful.  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-125/
- **A different reading (Barnes):** He offers two options. One is that God will not give His people the kind of prosperity the wicked enjoy, and keeps them upright through trial. The other is that oppressive rule will not last.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/125-3.htm

### v. 4: "Do good, O LORD, to those who are good"

**Traditional reading**
- **Guzik:** The psalmist asks God to keep the Sinai covenant's pattern of blessing obedience. The gospel goes further: God did good to those who are *not* good (Rom. 5:6, 8).  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-125/
- **Gill:** "The good" are those whom God's Spirit and grace have made good, for none are naturally good. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/125.htm
- **Pulpit Commentary:** The second line explains the first: Only the "upright in heart" are really "good." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/125.htm
- **Spurgeon:** The prayer is really a promise in another form.  His *Treasury* also links "do good" to Nehemiah, notes that "upright" literally means "straight," and points out the psalm's five names for God's people.  https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps125.cfm
- **Benson:** The upright in heart are those who stay true to God's ways even while being disciplined and tested.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/benson/psalms/125.htm

### v. 5: "Those who turn to crooked ways… Peace be upon Israel"

**Traditional reading**
- **Pulpit Commentary:** The word for "crooked ways" appears only here and in Judges 5:6 and means "by-paths." The last line should be read as a prayer, "peace *be*," not a prediction.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/125.htm
- **Who is meant:**
  - Gill: not the openly wicked but carnal professors who give up their faith under persecution. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/125.htm
  - Henry: hypocrites and deserters. The psalmist predicts their ruin rather than praying for it.  https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_125.cfm
  - Spurgeon: time-servers will be led out to the same gallows as the openly wicked. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps125.cfm
- **"Peace":**
  - Gill sees "peace upon Israel" behind Galatians 6:16.  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/psalms-125.html
  - Spurgeon links the first and last verses: Israel trusts (v. 1), and Israel has peace (v. 5).  https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps125.cfm
  - Guzik pictures the wicked being led into exile, and calls the closing line a priestly blessing.   https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-125/

## Where Protestant traditions differ: vv. 1–3 and 5 (can a true believer fall away?)

- **Reformed / Puritan (John Owen, quoted in Spurgeon's *Treasury*):** Verses 1–2 are a straightforward promise that believers will stay in God's favour. They are not a reward offered on the condition that they keep going.  https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps125.cfm
- **Baptist (Spurgeon, Gill):**
  - Spurgeon: the two verses prove the eternal safety of the saints. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps125.cfm
  - Gill: believers may lose the felt sense of God's presence, but never lose their state of grace.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/125.htm
- **Reformed (Calvin):** Even if our own strength fails, God will see to it that we do not abandon His service. Calvin also warns that no one has enough strength to last to the end unless God cares for our weakness.  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/psalms-125.html
- **A more conditional reading (Pulpit Commentary):**
  - On v. 2, God is always around His true people, "though he may have to forsake those who have first forsaken him."  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/125.htm
  - On v. 3, the danger is that the righteous lose patience "and fall from grace."  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/125-3.htm
- **Guzik and Constable:** Both stress trust as a condition. Constable's note says believers are secure, but warns God's people to follow Him faithfully or lose His blessing.  https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/125-1.html
- **Lutheran (Luther, quoted in Jamieson-Fausset-Brown):** On v. 3, God may test His people to the limit. When only despair is left, He rescues them and gives life in death.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/125-3.htm

Note: I could not read Wesley's own notes or a Methodist source on this psalm, so the Wesleyan/Arminian view is not given in its own teachers' words here.

## Other views

- **Modern scholarship:**
  - The NET Bible's note on v. 3: a "scepter of wickedness" means an oppressive foreign conqueror. The NET also notes that pilgrims may have recited these psalms on the road up to Jerusalem.  https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php/d/xml/bible.php?book=Psa&chapter=125
  - The NET translates v. 5 as a wish: "may the Lord remove them."  https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Psa&chapter=125
  - The Cambridge Bible (quoted on Biblehub) dates v. 3 to Nehemiah's time, when Samaritans harassed the Jews with Persian approval. It adds that "the wicked" (KJV, following the Greek Septuagint) versus the Hebrew "wickedness" is a difference of vowel points only.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/125-3.htm
  - Bob Utley (bible.org): the time frame of v. 3 is uncertain, and the ruler could be a foreign pagan or an idolatrous Israelite king.  https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-125
  - Coffman: the "scepter" means renegade Jews who had sided with a foreign power.  https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/125-5.html
- **Catholic (Augustine, in the Church Fathers collection on New Advent):**
  - He reads the surrounding mountains as the holy Scriptures, through which help comes. 
  - On v. 3, he tells good servants of bad masters to endure for a time, because that rule is not forever. 
  - On v. 5, Christ is peace, and he warns against those who wish to tear unity asunder.
  - https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801125.htm
  - The Catholic Douay-Rheims and Brenton's Septuagint translation add "the Lord" as subject in v. 3: "the Lord will not leave the rod of sinners…"  https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/net/psalms/125-3.html

**Not found:** Orthodox (oca.org) readings, Wesley's own notes, a Pentecostal or Anglican writer speaking for their tradition, and any prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching on this psalm. A different search would be needed for those. The closest point I found is Barnes's comment on v. 3, which says God does *not* give His people prosperity the way He gives it to the wicked.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/125-3.htm
